Whoever controls how long a signal persists controls whether a coordinating network can be mapped after the fact. Coordination through public signs is only as safe as participants’ control over decay, or the control of a third party bound to published rules.

Research on stigmergy treats evaporation as a property of the medium. On digital platforms, evaporation is a retention policy set by an owner, and signals that fade for participants can persist for someone else.
Networks whose signals are retained by third parties prove no easier to reconstruct or disrupt than comparable networks whose signals actually expire.
A public schedule lowers coordination costs for members and raises exposure to anyone else who can read it. Predictable timing gets gamed by the measured and exploited by adversaries.

US nursing homes slack after an inspection and ramp up before the next. In 2003 about a third of their inspections were predictable in timing, partly because of the maximum-interval rule itself. Ransomware groups have timed major attacks to holiday weekends.
